core: Labor demand is a DERIVED demand: firms hire workers not for their own sake but because of the value of what those workers produce, so labor demand depends on the demand for the firm's output.

The marginal revenue product of labor (MRP) is the extra revenue one more worker brings; in a perfectly competitive output market it equals the value of the marginal product, VMP = marginal product of labor x output price (MRP = MP x MR more generally).
A profit-maximizing firm hires additional labor up to the point where the wage equals the marginal revenue product (VMP) of the last worker.
Labor supply slopes upward in the wage: at higher wages more workers/hours are offered to a given labor market (with the income/substitution nuance noted briefly).
The equilibrium wage and employment level occur where market labor demand equals market labor supply.

Wages differ because of productivity and human capital (education, training, experience, skill), compensating differentials for unpleasant or dangerous work, and discrimination as a factor; much of observed wage gaps reflects productivity/human-capital differences, but not all.

A neutral, brief note that a labor union bargains collectively over wages and conditions, and that a minimum wage is a legally set wage floor (a price floor) whose binding effects are analyzed by the price-controls topic.
supporting: MRP builds on the marginal product of labor, which the production topic owns.
Because a compensating differential is what workers require to accept worse conditions, it operates through labor supply: undesirable jobs must offer higher pay to attract the same workers.
Income effect vs substitution effect can bend individual labor supply backward at very high wages, but the market labor-supply curve is treated as upward sloping.
outOfScope: The minimum-wage price-floor analysis and surplus/shortage mechanics (economics:foundations:price-controls owns this).
The marginal product of labor and diminishing returns as a production concept (economics:foundations:production).
The general supply-and-demand model and market equilibrium mechanics (economics:foundations:supply, :demand).
Unemployment measurement, types, and the natural rate (economics:foundations:unemployment).

claims.claim: The demand for labor is a derived demand: it depends on the demand for the product the firm produces, because a firm hires workers for the value of their marginal productivity, not for labor in itself.

In a perfectly competitive output market the firm's demand for labor equals the value of the marginal product of labor, VMP = marginal product of labor multiplied by the output price; when the firm has market power the relevant concept is the marginal revenue product, MRP = marginal product of labor multiplied by marginal revenue.

A profit-maximizing firm hires labor up to the point where the market wage equals the marginal revenue product (in competitive output markets, where the wage equals the value of the marginal product of labor).
The labor supply curve is an upward-sloping function of the wage rate: higher wages attract more workers to a particular labor market.

The equilibrium wage and quantity of labor are determined where market labor demand equals market labor supply; at that wage every employer willing to hire at the equilibrium wage finds a worker and every worker willing to work at that wage finds a job.
Education and training raise a worker's productivity and shift labor demand and supply, and are among the factors that make equilibrium wages differ across labor markets.

Labor-market discrimination occurs when workers with comparable education, experience, and expertise are paid differently because of characteristics such as gender or race; lower average education for some groups explains part of an earnings gap, so not every wage gap is the product of overt discrimination, yet gaps that persist among comparably qualified workers point to discrimination as a factor.
A labor union is an organization of workers that negotiates as a group with employers over compensation and working conditions; U.S. union membership has declined over time.
A minimum wage is a legally set wage floor; as a price floor it binds only when set above the equilibrium wage, and the analysis of the resulting labor surplus belongs to the price-controls topic.

Worked example (arithmetic independently verified): a firm sells output at $2 per unit; marginal products of the 1st-5th workers are 20, 18, 14, 10, 6 units, giving values of the marginal product of $40, $36, $28, $20, $12; at a wage of $22 per worker the firm hires 3 workers, because the 3rd worker's VMP ($28) exceeds the wage while the 4th worker's VMP ($20) is below it.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How much of observed wage gaps between demographic groups reflects discrimination versus differences in human capital and job characteristics.
positions: Part of measured earnings gaps reflects differences in average education, experience, and occupation (human-capital and productivity factors).
Gaps that persist among workers with comparable education, experience, and expertise are evidence that discrimination remains a factor.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both: it teaches that productivity and human capital explain much of why wages differ, and that discrimination is a documented additional factor, without asserting a single percentage split. The topic is labeled as involving contested measurement.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether individual labor supply always rises with the wage.
positions: Standard market labor-supply curves slope upward: higher wages draw more workers and hours.
For an individual, a high enough wage can trigger a backward-bending supply as the income effect outweighs the substitution effect.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the upward-sloping market supply curve as the working model and notes the income/substitution nuance briefly, as the brief directs.
